content: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are a group of Gram-positive, non-sporulating, non-respiring, rod-shaped or coccoid bacteria that are characterized by their low-GC content and acid tolerance. These bacteria are metabolically and physiologically similar, producing lactic acid as the primary end product of carbohydrate fermentation. LAB are commonly found in decomposing plant material and dairy products. The production of lactic acid by LAB has historically been associated with food fermentation processes, as the acidification inhibits the growth of spoilage organisms. Additionally, many LAB strains produce proteinaceous bacteriocins, which serve as an additional barrier against spoilage and pathogenic microorganisms. Lactic acid and other metabolic byproducts of LAB contribute significantly to the sensory and textural properties of fermented foods. LAB are industrially important due to their Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) status, their widespread presence in food, and their role in maintaining healthy mucosal microflora in humans. The core genera of LAB include Lactobacillus, Leuconostoc, Pediococcus, Lactococcus, and Streptococcus, with additional genera such as Aerococcus, Carnobacterium, Enterococcus, Oenococcus, Tetragenococcus, Vagococcus, and Weissella. These genera belong to the order Lactobacillales. LAB are characterized by their ability to tolerate low pH environments, which is a result of their acid production (e.g., lactic acid). In laboratory settings, media used to culture LAB typically include a carbohydrate source, as most LAB species are incapable of respiration. LAB metabolism is classified into two main hexose fermentation pathways: homolactic and heterolactic fermentation. Homolactic LAB metabolize glucose via the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas (EMP) pathway, producing two molecules of pyruvate per glucose molecule. Intracellular redox balance is maintained by oxidizing NADH, coupled with the reduction of pyruvate to lactic acid. This process generates two molecules of ATP per glucose molecule. Representative homolactic LAB genera include Lactococcus, Enterococcus, Streptococcus, Pediococcus, and Group I Lactobacilli. Heterofermentative LAB utilize the pentose phosphate pathway (also known as the phosphoketolase pathway). In this pathway, glucose-6-phosphate is dehydrogenated to 6-phosphogluconate and subsequently decarboxylated to produce one molecule of CO₂. The resulting pentose-5-phosphate is cleaved into one molecule of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (GAP) and one molecule of acetyl phosphate. GAP is further metabolized to lactate, while acetyl phosphate is reduced to ethanol via acetyl-CoA and acetaldehyde intermediates. Theoretically, the end products (including ATP) are produced in equimolar quantities from the metabolism of one glucose molecule. Obligate heterofermentative LAB include Leuconostoc, Oenococcus, Weissella, and Group III Lactobacilli. In 1985, the genus Streptococcus was reclassified into Lactococcus, Enterococcus, Vagococcus, and Streptococcus based on biochemical and molecular characteristics. Historically, streptococci were classified primarily by serology, which aligns well with current taxonomic definitions. Lactococci (formerly Lancefield Group N streptococci) are extensively used as starter cultures in dairy fermentations, with humans estimated to consume 10¹⁸ lactococci annually. Due to their industrial relevance, Lactococcus lactis subspecies (lactis and cremoris) are widely used as model organisms for LAB research. For example, L. lactis ssp. cremoris, used in hard cheese production, is represented by laboratory strains LM0230 and MG1363. Similarly, L. lactis ssp. lactis is employed in soft cheese fermentations, with strain IL1403 being a prominent model in LAB research. The genome of IL1403 was sequenced in 2001, marking a significant shift in resources toward understanding LAB genomics and applications. Currently, two publicly available genome sequences of L. lactis ssp. cremoris exist. In industrial bacterial fermentation, large-scale cultivation of bacteria is used to produce food products, commodity chemicals, and biotechnological products. However, the risk of bacteriophage contamination poses a significant threat to these processes, as phages can rapidly halt fermentations and cause economic losses. The interaction between bacteriophages and their bacterial hosts is critical in the context of the food fermentation industry. Efforts to control phage propagation and dissemination, as well as the development of biotechnological defense strategies, are of great interest. The dairy fermentation industry has long recognized the problem of phages and has collaborated with academia and starter culture companies to develop strategies to limit phage propagation and evolution. The initial interaction between a bacteriophage and its bacterial host involves the attachment of the phage to the host cell. This attachment is mediated by the phage's receptor-binding protein (RBP), which recognizes and binds to a receptor on the bacterial surface. RBPs are also referred to as host specificity proteins, host determinants, or anti-receptors. Various molecules, including polysaccharides, (lipo)teichoic acids, and single membrane proteins, have been suggested as host receptors for LAB-infecting phages. Several RBPs of LAB phages have been identified through the generation of hybrid phages with altered host ranges. These studies have also identified additional phage proteins that are important for successful infection. Structural analysis of RBPs has revealed a common tertiary folding pattern and supports the saccharide nature of the host receptor. Gram-positive LAB possess a thick peptidoglycan layer, which must be traversed for the phage genome to be injected into the bacterial cytoplasm. Peptidoglycan-degrading enzymes, often structural components of LAB phages, facilitate this penetration. Probiotics are products designed to deliver live, potentially beneficial bacterial cells to the gut ecosystem of humans and animals. Prebiotics, on the other hand, are non-digestible carbohydrates that serve as fermentable substrates for specific bacteria in the large intestine. LAB strains are the most commonly used microbes in probiotic formulations. Two principal genera of probiotic/prebiotic bacteria, Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, have been extensively studied.
